name: a force
short: A force is a push or a pull. Forces can make things start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, change direction or change shape. Forces are measured in newtons (N).

sections.p: Kicking a ball is a push. Opening a drawer is a pull. Gravity pulls you down towards the Earth. Every force acts in a direction, so we draw forces as arrows: the longer the arrow, the bigger the force.
**Contact forces** need things to touch: friction, air resistance, and the push of your hand. **Non-contact forces** act across a gap: gravity, magnetic force and static electric force.

If the forces on an object are balanced (equal and opposite), its motion does not change: it stays still or keeps moving at the same speed. If they are unbalanced, it speeds up, slows down or changes direction.

examples: Gravity pulls a dropped apple down.
Friction slows a sliding book.
A magnet pulls a paper clip without touching it.
mistake: Thinking a moving object always needs a force to keep it moving. If the forces are balanced, a moving object keeps moving at a steady speed.

quiz.q: Which is a non-contact force?
quiz.explain: Gravity acts across a gap: the Earth pulls you even when you jump in the air.

quiz.q: What unit are forces measured in?
quiz.explain: Forces are measured in newtons, named after Isaac Newton.

faq: What are the main types of forces?
Gravity (weight), friction, air resistance, water resistance, upthrust, magnetic force, tension and the push or pull of an object.

name: gravity
short: Gravity is a force that pulls objects with mass towards each other. The Earth's gravity pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth, which is why things fall down.

sections.p: Everything that has mass pulls on everything else, but the pull is only big when the mass is huge, like a planet or a star. That's why you notice the Earth pulling you, but not your pencil.
Your weight is the force of gravity on you, measured in newtons. On Earth, each kilogram of mass weighs about 10 N. So a 30 kg child weighs about 300 N.

Gravity keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth and the Earth in orbit around the Sun. The Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's (about one sixth), so you would weigh less there, but your mass would be the same.

examples: A ball thrown up comes back down.
The Moon orbits the Earth.
An astronaut weighs less on the Moon than on Earth.
mistake: Thinking there is no gravity in space. Astronauts in orbit float because they are falling around the Earth all the time, not because gravity has gone.

quiz.q: Which direction does Earth's gravity pull you?
options: Towards the centre of the Earth
quiz.explain: Gravity pulls towards the centre of the Earth, which we call “down”.

quiz.q: On the Moon, what stays the same as on Earth?
quiz.explain: Mass is the amount of stuff in you and doesn't change. Your weight is smaller because the Moon's gravity is weaker.

faq: Who discovered gravity?
People always knew things fall, but Isaac Newton explained in the 1680s that the same force makes apples fall and keeps the Moon in orbit.

name: the difference between mass and weight
title: What is the difference between mass and weight?
short: Mass is how much matter (stuff) is in an object, measured in kilograms. Weight is the force of gravity pulling on that mass, measured in newtons. Your mass is the same everywhere; your weight changes with gravity.

sections.p: Mass is measured in grams (g) or kilograms (kg). A 2 kg bag of flour has a mass of 2 kg on Earth, on the Moon and in space.
Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons (N). On Earth, gravity pulls about 10 N on each kilogram. So the 2 kg bag weighs about 20 N here.
In everyday talk people say “I weigh 35 kg”, but scientists would say “my mass is 35 kg” and “my weight is about 350 N”.

examples: An astronaut with a mass of 70 kg weighs about 700 N on Earth.
On the Moon the same astronaut still has a mass of 70 kg, but weighs only about 115 N.
mistake: Writing weight in kilograms. In science, weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons.

quiz.q: What is weight measured in?
quiz.explain: Weight is a force, and forces are measured in newtons.

quiz.q: About how much does a 5 kg bag weigh on Earth?
quiz.explain: Each kilogram weighs about 10 N on Earth: 5 × 10 = 50 N.

faq: Would I weigh less on the Moon?
Yes. The Moon's gravity is about one sixth of Earth's, so your weight would be about one sixth. Your mass would not change.

name: friction
short: Friction is a force that acts when two surfaces rub or slide against each other. It always works against the movement, so it slows things down. It also heats the surfaces up.

sections.p: Rough surfaces like carpet or sandpaper make more friction. Smooth surfaces like ice make very little. Even surfaces that look smooth have tiny bumps that catch on each other.
Without friction we could not walk (our shoes would slip), cars could not brake, and pencils could not write. Tyres and shoe soles have patterns to grip better.
Friction wastes energy as heat and wears things out. Oil in a bike chain reduces friction, so the parts move more easily.

examples: Rubbing your hands together makes them warm.
A sledge slides further on ice than on grass.
Brakes use friction to stop a bike.
mistake: Thinking friction only slows things down. Friction is also what lets your feet push you forward when you walk.

quiz.q: On which surface would a toy car roll furthest?
quiz.explain: Smooth tiles make the least friction, so the car slows down the least.

quiz.q: Why do we put oil on a bike chain?
quiz.explain: Oil lets the parts slide past each other easily, so less energy is wasted.

faq: Is air resistance a type of friction?
Yes. Air resistance (drag) is friction between a moving object and the air. Water resistance is the same idea in water.

name: energy
short: Energy is what is needed to make things happen. It is stored in different ways (energy stores) and moved from one store to another when something happens. Energy is measured in joules (J).

sections.p: Some stores: **kinetic** (moving things), **chemical** (food, fuel, batteries), **thermal** (hot things), **gravitational** (things lifted up high), **elastic** (stretched or squashed springs) and **nuclear**.
When you eat breakfast and then run, energy moves from the chemical store in the food to your muscles, and then to the kinetic store as you move. Some always ends up heating the surroundings.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only moved between stores. This is called the **conservation of energy**. Energy that spreads out as heat is still there, just not useful any more.

examples: A battery's chemical store is transferred to light in a torch.
A ball held high has a gravitational store; dropped, it gains kinetic energy.
A kettle transfers energy electrically to the thermal store of the water.
mistake: Saying energy gets “used up”. It is never used up; it is transferred, and often ends up spread out as heat.

quiz.q: Which store does a moving car have lots of?
quiz.explain: Kinetic is the energy store of moving things.

quiz.q: What unit is energy measured in?
quiz.explain: Energy is measured in joules. Watts measure power: how fast energy is transferred.

faq: What is the difference between energy and power?
Energy is how much is transferred (joules). Power is how fast it is transferred (watts). A 100 W bulb transfers 100 J every second.

name: density
short: Density is how much mass is packed into a certain volume. A brick is denser than a sponge of the same size. Density = mass ÷ volume, often in g/cm³.

sections.p: Dense materials have their particles packed closely together, or have heavy particles. Lead is very dense; polystyrene is not.
Density = mass ÷ volume. A block with a mass of 40 g and a volume of 20 cm³ has a density of 40 ÷ 20 = 2 g/cm³.
Water has a density of 1 g/cm³. Objects less dense than water float; objects denser than water sink. Wood floats, a steel bolt sinks.

examples: Ice (about 0.92 g/cm³) floats on water.
Gold is about 19 times as dense as water.
Oil floats on water because it is less dense.
mistake: Thinking heavy things always sink. A huge ship is heavy, but it floats because its overall density (steel plus all the air inside) is less than water's.

quiz.q: A block has a mass of 30 g and a volume of 10 cm³. What is its density?
quiz.explain: Density = mass ÷ volume = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 g/cm³.

quiz.q: Which will float in water?
quiz.explain: Anything less dense than water (1 g/cm³) floats.

faq: Why does ice float?
Water expands when it freezes, so ice is less dense than liquid water. That's why ice cubes float and ponds freeze from the top down.

name: the states of matter
title: What are the states of matter: solids, liquids and gases?
short: Matter can be a solid, a liquid or a gas. In a solid the particles are packed tightly in fixed places, in a liquid they are close but can slide past each other, and in a gas they are far apart and move quickly in all directions.

sections.p: Solids keep their shape and can't be squashed. Their particles are close together in a regular pattern and only vibrate on the spot.
Liquids flow and take the shape of their container, but keep the same volume. Their particles are close together but can move past each other.
Gases spread out to fill any container and can be squashed. Their particles are far apart and move fast in random directions.
Heating: solid → liquid is **melting**, liquid → gas is **evaporating** (or boiling). Cooling: gas → liquid is **condensing**, liquid → solid is **freezing**. Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

examples: Ice (solid), water (liquid) and steam (gas) are all water.
Chocolate melts in your hand.
Water droplets form on a cold window: condensation.
mistake: Thinking particles get bigger when something melts or boils. The particles stay the same size; they move faster and further apart.

quiz.q: Which state of matter can be squashed easily?
quiz.explain: Gas particles are far apart, so there is lots of space to push them into.

quiz.q: What is it called when a gas turns into a liquid?
quiz.explain: Condensing, like steam turning into drops of water on a cold mirror.

faq: Are there more than three states of matter?
At school we study three: solid, liquid and gas. Scientists also describe plasma (found in stars and lightning), but you don't need it at KS3.

name: diffusion
short: Diffusion is the spreading out of particles from where there are lots of them to where there are fewer, because the particles move about randomly. It happens in liquids and gases.

sections.p: When someone opens a bottle of perfume, you smell it across the room a little later. The perfume particles mix with the air particles and spread out by themselves.
Particles move randomly in all directions. Overall, more of them move from where they are crowded to where they are spread out, until they are evenly mixed.
Heat makes particles move faster, so diffusion is quicker in hot water than in cold. It is fastest in gases and very slow in solids.

examples: A drop of food colouring slowly spreads through a glass of water.
The smell of toast spreads through a house.
Oxygen diffuses from your lungs into your blood.
mistake: Thinking you need to stir for diffusion to happen. Stirring speeds up mixing, but diffusion happens on its own.

quiz.q: In which will food colouring spread fastest?
quiz.explain: Particles move fastest in hot water, so diffusion is quickest.

quiz.q: Diffusion is particles moving from...
options: where there are many to where there are few
where there are few to where there are many
quiz.explain: Overall, particles spread from high concentration to low concentration.

faq: Does diffusion happen in solids?
Hardly at all at room temperature, because the particles in a solid can only vibrate in place.

name: static electricity
short: Static electricity is a build-up of electric charge on the surface of an object. It happens when two materials rub together and tiny particles called electrons move from one to the other.

sections.p: Rub a balloon on your hair and electrons move from your hair to the balloon. The balloon gets a **negative** charge, and your hair is left with a **positive** charge.
Opposite charges attract (pull together), like charges repel (push apart). That's why your hair stands up towards the balloon, and why two charged balloons push each other away.
If enough charge builds up, it can jump across a gap as a spark. Lightning is a giant spark from charged clouds.

examples: A rubbed balloon sticks to a wall.
You get a small shock touching a door handle after walking on carpet.
Lightning in a storm.
mistake: Thinking positive charges move when things are rubbed. In solids it is the negative electrons that move.

quiz.q: Two balloons both have a negative charge. What happens when they are brought close?
quiz.explain: Like charges repel, so they push apart.

quiz.q: What moves when a balloon is rubbed on hair?
quiz.explain: Electrons move from the hair to the balloon.

faq: Why is it called static?
Static means not moving. The charge stays put on the surface instead of flowing as a current.

name: a series and a parallel circuit
title: What is the difference between series and parallel circuits?
short: In a series circuit all the parts are joined in one single loop. In a parallel circuit there is more than one loop (branch), so the current splits and each branch works on its own.

sections.p: There is only one path. If one bulb breaks, the loop is broken and everything goes off. Adding more bulbs in series makes each one dimmer.
Each bulb has its own branch to the cell. If one bulb breaks, the others stay on. Bulbs in parallel stay bright when you add more (but the cell runs down faster).
The lights and sockets in a house are wired in parallel, so you can switch one off without the others going off too.

examples: Old Christmas lights were often in series: one broken bulb made the whole string go out.
Car headlights are in parallel: if one fails, the other still works.
mistake: Thinking the current gets “used up” by the first bulb in a series circuit. The current is the same all the way round a series loop.

quiz.q: In which circuit does one broken bulb make all the others go off?
quiz.explain: A series circuit has one loop, so a break stops the current everywhere.

quiz.q: Why are homes wired in parallel?
options: So each light can be switched on and off on its own
quiz.explain: Each branch works independently.

faq: Where does the current split?
In a parallel circuit, the current splits where the wire branches and joins up again afterwards. The currents in the branches add up to the total.

name: refraction
short: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one material into another, such as from air into water or glass. It happens because light changes speed.

sections.p: Light travels more slowly in water and glass than in air. When it hits the surface at an angle, the change in speed makes it change direction.
A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface. The straw is straight; the light coming from the part under water bends as it leaves the water.
Lenses use refraction to bend light on purpose. Glasses, magnifying glasses, cameras and your own eyes all have lenses.

examples: A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.
A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger.
A prism splits white light into a rainbow spectrum.
mistake: Mixing up refraction and reflection. Reflection is light bouncing off a surface; refraction is light bending as it goes through into a new material.

quiz.q: Why does a straw look bent in water?
options: Light bends as it leaves the water
quiz.explain: That bending of light is refraction.

quiz.q: What causes refraction?
quiz.explain: Light slows down or speeds up as it enters a new material, which bends it.

faq: How does refraction make a rainbow?
Each colour in white light bends by a slightly different amount, so a prism or raindrops spread the colours out into a spectrum.

name: a light year
short: A light year is a distance, not a time. It is how far light travels in one year: about 9.5 million million kilometres (9.5 trillion km).

sections.p: Light travels about 300,000 km every second. It reaches us from the Sun in about 8 minutes, and could go round the Earth more than 7 times in one second.
Space is so huge that kilometres give enormous numbers. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light years away. That's about 40 trillion km.
When you see a star 100 light years away, the light left it 100 years ago. You are seeing the star as it was then.

examples: Light from the Moon takes just over 1 second to reach us.
The Milky Way galaxy is about 100,000 light years across.
mistake: Thinking a light year is a length of time because it has “year” in it. It measures distance.

quiz.q: What does a light year measure?
quiz.explain: It is the distance light travels in one year.

quiz.q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
quiz.explain: The Sun is about 150 million km away; light takes about 8 minutes.

faq: How far is a light year in km?
About 9.46 million million km, often rounded to about 9.5 trillion km.

name: an element, a compound and a mixture
title: What is an element, a compound and a mixture?
short: An element is made of only one type of atom. A compound is two or more elements chemically joined together. A mixture is different substances mixed but not joined, so they can be separated again.

sections.p: There are about 118 elements, listed in the periodic table. Each has a symbol: O for oxygen, Fe for iron, Au for gold. An element can't be split into anything simpler by chemical reactions.

In a compound, atoms of different elements are bonded together in a fixed ratio. Water (H₂O) has 2 hydrogen atoms joined to 1 oxygen atom. A compound can be very different from its elements: sodium (a reactive metal) and chlorine (a poisonous gas) make sodium chloride, table salt.
In a mixture the substances are just mixed, not bonded. Salty water, air and sand with iron filings are mixtures. They can be separated by filtering, evaporating, using a magnet and so on.

examples: Element: oxygen, gold, carbon.
Compound: water, carbon dioxide, table salt.
Mixture: air, sea water, a salad.
mistake: Thinking air is a compound. Air is a mixture of gases (mostly nitrogen and oxygen) that are not bonded to each other.

quiz.q: Which of these is an element?
quiz.explain: Iron is made of only one type of atom. Water and salt are compounds; air is a mixture.

quiz.q: Which can be separated by filtering?
quiz.explain: Sand and water is a mixture; the sand stays in the filter paper. Compounds can't be separated by filtering.

faq: What is the smallest part of an element?
An atom. Every atom of the same element has the same number of protons.

name: an acid and an alkali
title: What are acids and alkalis? The pH scale explained
short: Acids and alkalis are chemical opposites. The pH scale from 0 to 14 shows how acidic or alkaline something is: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, and above 7 is alkaline.

sections.p: Acids have a pH below 7. Weak acids such as lemon juice and vinegar taste sour. Strong acids such as hydrochloric acid are corrosive and dangerous.
Alkalis have a pH above 7. Soap, toothpaste and baking soda solution are weak alkalis. Oven cleaner is a strong alkali, and is also corrosive.
Universal indicator changes colour with pH: red or orange for acids, green for neutral, blue or purple for alkalis. Red cabbage juice works as a home-made indicator.
When an acid and an alkali react, they cancel each other out, making a salt and water. Indigestion tablets neutralise extra stomach acid.

examples: Lemon juice: about pH 2 (acid).
Pure water: pH 7 (neutral).
Soap: about pH 9 to 10 (alkali).
mistake: Thinking all acids are dangerous. Many are weak and safe to eat, like the citric acid in oranges. Strong acids and alkalis are the dangerous ones.

quiz.q: A liquid has a pH of 3. What is it?
quiz.explain: Anything below pH 7 is acidic.

quiz.q: What colour does universal indicator go in a neutral solution?
quiz.explain: Neutral (pH 7) is green.

faq: What does neutral mean?
Neither acidic nor alkaline: pH 7, like pure water.

name: photosynthesis
short: Photosynthesis is how plants make their own food. They use energy from light to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose (a sugar), and give out oxygen.

sections.p: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. The energy comes from light, which is captured by a green substance called **chlorophyll**.
Mostly in the leaves, inside tiny parts of the cells called **chloroplasts**. Carbon dioxide enters through small holes in the leaf, and water comes up from the roots.
Photosynthesis makes the food at the start of almost every food chain, and it puts oxygen into the air for animals (and plants) to breathe.

examples: A plant left in the dark for days stops growing well.
Pondweed in light gives off bubbles of oxygen.
mistake: Thinking plants get their food from the soil. They take water and some minerals from the soil, but they make their food (glucose) themselves by photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Which gas do plants take in for photosynthesis?
quiz.explain: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.

quiz.q: What does chlorophyll do?
quiz.explain: Chlorophyll is the green substance that absorbs light.

faq: Do plants breathe?
Plants respire all the time, day and night, like animals: they use oxygen and give out carbon dioxide. In daylight, photosynthesis is usually faster, so overall they give out oxygen.

name: a food chain
short: A food chain shows what eats what, and how energy passes from one living thing to the next. It always starts with a plant (a producer), and the arrows point from the food to the animal that eats it.

sections.p: grass → rabbit → fox. The arrow means “is eaten by”, and it shows the direction the energy goes.

**Producer**: a plant that makes its own food (grass). **Primary consumer**: eats the producer (rabbit); it is a herbivore. **Secondary consumer**: eats the primary consumer (fox). **Predator** and **prey**: the fox is the predator, the rabbit is its prey.
Most animals eat more than one thing, so food chains join up into a food web. If one animal disappears, it can affect many others in the web.

examples: seaweed → winkle → crab → seagull
leaf → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk
mistake: Drawing the arrows the wrong way. The arrow points to the eater: grass → rabbit, not rabbit → grass.

quiz.q: In grass → rabbit → fox, which is the producer?
quiz.explain: The producer is the plant that makes its own food by photosynthesis.

quiz.q: In grass → rabbit → fox, what would probably happen if the foxes disappeared?
options: The number of rabbits would go up
quiz.explain: Fewer predators means more rabbits survive (and then they eat more grass).

faq: Why does a food chain start with a plant?
Plants make food using light energy from the Sun. Animals can't make their own food, so every chain starts with a producer.

name: a cell
short: A cell is the smallest living unit. All living things are made of cells. Most are too small to see without a microscope.

sections.p: An animal cell has a **nucleus** (controls the cell and holds the genetic material), **cytoplasm** (a jelly where reactions happen), a **cell membrane** (controls what goes in and out) and **mitochondria** (where respiration releases energy).
Plant cells have all of those, plus a **cell wall** (made of cellulose, for support), **chloroplasts** (for photosynthesis) and a large **vacuole** filled with cell sap.
Many cells have special shapes for their jobs. Red blood cells carry oxygen, nerve cells carry messages, and root hair cells take in water.

examples: Your body has tens of trillions of cells.
Bacteria are living things made of just one cell.
Onion skin cells are easy to see under a school microscope.
mistake: Thinking all cells have a cell wall. Plant cells (and bacteria and fungi) do, but animal cells don't.

quiz.q: Which part do plant cells have but animal cells don't?
quiz.explain: Chloroplasts (for photosynthesis) are only in plant cells. Plant cells also have a cell wall.

quiz.q: What does the nucleus do?
options: Gives the cell a stiff shape
quiz.explain: The nucleus contains the genetic material and controls what the cell does.

faq: Who discovered cells?
Robert Hooke named cells in 1665, after looking at thin slices of cork through an early microscope.

name: an atom
short: An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. Everything around you is made of atoms, and they are so small that about ten million of them in a line would only be 1 millimetre long.

sections.p: In the middle is a tiny **nucleus** made of **protons** and **neutrons**. Even tinier **electrons** move around the nucleus. Most of an atom is empty space.
Protons have a positive charge, electrons have a negative charge and neutrons have no charge. An atom has the same number of protons and electrons, so overall it has no charge.
An element is made of only one type of atom. What makes each element different is the number of protons: every hydrogen atom has 1 proton, every carbon atom has 6 and every oxygen atom has 8.

examples: A gold ring is made of gold atoms only.
Oxygen in the air is made of oxygen atoms joined in pairs.
Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms joined together.
mistake: Mixing up atoms and cells. Cells are the building blocks of living things and you can see them with a microscope. Atoms are far, far smaller, and cells are made of billions of atoms.

quiz.q: Which part of an atom has a negative charge?
quiz.explain: Electrons are negative, protons are positive and neutrons have no charge.

quiz.q: Where are the protons and neutrons?
quiz.explain: Protons and neutrons are packed together in the nucleus, in the middle of the atom.

quiz.q: What makes a carbon atom different from an oxygen atom?
quiz.explain: Each element has its own number of protons: carbon has 6 and oxygen has 8.

faq: Can you see an atom?
Not with your eyes or a school microscope. Scientists can make pictures of atoms with special microscopes that use electrons instead of light.
Are atoms alive?
No. Atoms are not alive, but living things are made of atoms, just like everything else.

name: the periodic table
title: What is the periodic table?
short: The periodic table is a chart of all the known elements, 118 of them, in order of how many protons their atoms have. Elements with similar properties sit in the same column.

sections.p: The rows are called **periods** and the columns are called **groups**. Elements in the same group behave in similar ways. For example, the elements in Group 1, like sodium and potassium, are soft metals that react with water.

Most elements are metals, and they are on the left and in the middle. The non-metals, like oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine, are on the right. The last column holds the noble gases, like helium and neon, which hardly react at all.

Each element has a symbol of one or two letters. The first letter is always a capital: O is oxygen, C is carbon and Ca is calcium. Some come from old Latin names: Na is sodium (natrium) and Fe is iron (ferrum).

examples: H is hydrogen, the first element, with 1 proton.
Au is gold, from the Latin word aurum.
Helium (He) is a noble gas, used in party balloons.
mistake: Thinking every symbol is the first letter or two of the English name. Many are, but some come from Latin: K is potassium, Pb is lead and Ag is silver.

quiz.q: What is the symbol for sodium?
quiz.explain: Sodium is Na, from its Latin name natrium. S is sulfur.

quiz.q: What are the columns of the periodic table called?
quiz.explain: Columns are groups and rows are periods. Elements in a group have similar properties.

quiz.q: Where are most of the metals?
options: On the left and in the middle
quiz.explain: Metals are on the left and in the middle; non-metals are on the right.

faq: Who made the periodic table?
The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published a famous version in 1869. He left gaps for elements nobody had found yet, and he predicted what they would be like.
How many elements are there?
118 elements are known so far. About 90 are found in nature; the rest have been made by scientists.

name: a chemical reaction
short: A chemical reaction is a change that makes new substances. The atoms of the starting substances join up in new ways, and no atoms are made or destroyed.

sections.p: Look for a colour change, bubbles of gas, the mixture getting hot or cold, light or a flame, or a solid appearing in a liquid. These clues tell you a new substance may have formed.
We write reactions as word equations. The starting substances (**reactants**) go on the left and the new substances (**products**) on the right: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.

In a **physical change**, like melting ice or dissolving sugar, no new substance is made and it is usually easy to undo. A **chemical change** makes something new and is usually hard to undo: you can't un-bake a cake.

examples: Burning wood makes ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Iron rusting: iron + oxygen + water → rust.
Baking powder in a cake mix gives off carbon dioxide bubbles that make the cake rise.
mistake: Thinking mass is lost in a reaction. If a gas escapes into the air the mixture looks lighter, but if you catch everything in a closed container the total mass stays the same.

quiz.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
quiz.explain: Burning makes new substances (ash, gases). The others make nothing new.

quiz.q: In 'magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide', what is magnesium oxide?
quiz.explain: Products are the new substances on the right of the arrow.

faq: Is cooking a chemical reaction?
Often, yes. Frying an egg, toasting bread and baking a cake all make new substances that you can't turn back into the raw ingredients.
Is dissolving a chemical reaction?
No. Dissolving is a physical change: the salt or sugar is still there in the water, and you can get it back by evaporating the water.

name: combustion
short: Combustion is the scientific word for burning. A fuel reacts with oxygen and gives out energy as heat and light.

sections.p: A fire needs three things: **fuel**, **heat** and **oxygen**. Take away any one of them and the fire goes out. A fire blanket works by cutting off the oxygen.
Many fuels, like natural gas, petrol and candle wax, contain carbon and hydrogen. When they burn with plenty of oxygen they make carbon dioxide and water: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

With too little oxygen, burning can make soot and **carbon monoxide**. Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas with no colour and no smell, which is why homes with gas boilers should have a carbon monoxide alarm.

examples: A candle burning wax.
A gas cooker burning natural gas (methane).
A campfire burning wood.
mistake: Thinking things always get lighter when they burn. Wood seems to lose mass because its products are gases that escape. When iron wool burns it gets heavier, because it joins with oxygen from the air to make iron oxide.

quiz.q: Which gas from the air is needed for burning?
quiz.explain: Combustion is a reaction with oxygen.

quiz.q: How does a fire blanket put out a small fire?
quiz.explain: Covering the fire stops oxygen reaching it, so one side of the fire triangle is gone.

faq: Is combustion a chemical reaction?
Yes. New substances are made, such as carbon dioxide and water, and energy is given out.
Why does blowing on a fire sometimes make it bigger?
Blowing gently brings more oxygen to the fuel, so it burns faster. Blowing hard on a small flame, like a candle, cools it and pushes the hot gases away, so it goes out.

name: dissolving
short: Dissolving is when a substance, like sugar, mixes completely into a liquid, like water, so you can't see it any more. The result is called a solution.

sections.p: The substance that dissolves is the **solute** (sugar). The liquid it dissolves in is the **solvent** (water). Together they make a **solution** (sugar water).
Something that dissolves is **soluble**, like salt and sugar. Something that doesn't is **insoluble**, like sand. When no more solute can dissolve, the solution is **saturated**.
Stirring, using warmer water and using smaller pieces (like caster sugar instead of sugar cubes) all make a solid dissolve faster. For most solids, warmer water can also dissolve more.

examples: Salt dissolving in sea water.
Instant coffee dissolving in hot water.
Squash mixing into water.
mistake: Saying sugar 'melts' in tea. Melting needs heat and only one substance, like ice turning to water. In tea the sugar dissolves: it is still there, spread out between the water particles, which is why the tea tastes sweet.

quiz.q: In salty water, which is the solvent?
quiz.explain: The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving: water.

quiz.q: You dissolve 10 g of salt in 100 g of water. What is the mass of the solution?
quiz.explain: Nothing is lost when something dissolves: 100 g + 10 g = 110 g.

quiz.q: Which of these is insoluble in water?
quiz.explain: Sand doesn't dissolve, so you can separate it from water by filtering.

faq: How do you get salt back from salty water?
Evaporate the water by leaving it in a warm place or heating it gently. The water turns to vapour and the salt crystals are left behind.
Is dissolving reversible?
Yes. Dissolving is a physical change, so you can get the solute back, for example by evaporation.

name: chromatography
short: Chromatography is a way to separate the different dyes in a mixture, like ink. The dyes travel up a strip of paper with a solvent such as water, and they spread out because each one travels a different distance.

sections.p: Draw a line in **pencil** near the bottom of a strip of filter paper and put a dot of ink on it. Stand the paper in a little water, with the water level **below** the line. Watch the water soak up the paper and carry the ink with it.
Each dye dissolves in the solvent a different amount and sticks to the paper a different amount. Dyes that dissolve well and don't stick much travel further up the paper.
The finished paper is called a **chromatogram**. A pure substance makes one spot. A mixture makes several spots. If two spots are at the same height, they could be the same dye.

examples: Finding out which colours are mixed in a black felt-tip pen.
Checking which food colourings are in a sweet.
Matching ink from a note to the pen that wrote it.
mistake: Putting the ink dot below the water level, or drawing the line in pen. The ink then dissolves straight into the water in the beaker, and the pen line runs too. Use pencil, which doesn't dissolve, and keep the line above the water.

quiz.q: Why is the start line drawn in pencil?
options: Pencil doesn't dissolve in the solvent
Pencil makes the dyes move faster
Pens are not allowed in labs
quiz.explain: Pencil is made of graphite, which doesn't dissolve, so it won't run up the paper and confuse the result.

quiz.q: A sample makes three spots. What does that tell you?
options: It is a mixture of at least three dyes
quiz.explain: Each spot is a different substance, so a sample with three spots contains at least three dyes.

faq: Can I do chromatography at home?
Yes, with an adult's OK. Use a strip of kitchen roll or a coffee filter, a felt-tip pen dot and a glass with a little water. Black and brown felt-tips often give the most surprising colours.
What does chromatography mean?
It comes from Greek words meaning 'colour writing', because the first experiments separated coloured substances from plants.

name: respiration
short: Respiration is a chemical reaction that happens in every living cell. It releases energy from glucose (a sugar from food) so the cell can move, grow and stay alive.

sections.p: With oxygen, cells release energy from glucose: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. This mostly happens in tiny parts of the cell called **mitochondria**.

Without enough oxygen, for example when you sprint hard, muscle cells can release a little energy without oxygen: glucose → lactic acid. Yeast does it differently: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide, and the carbon dioxide bubbles make bread rise.

Breathing brings oxygen into your lungs and takes carbon dioxide out. The blood carries the oxygen to every cell and brings the carbon dioxide back. So breathing and respiration are linked, but they are not the same thing.

examples: Your muscle cells respiring when you run.
Plants respiring all the time, day and night.
Yeast respiring in bread dough.
mistake: Thinking respiration means breathing. Breathing is moving air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is the reaction inside cells that releases energy, and plants and bacteria do it too, even though they don't have lungs.

quiz.q: Which are the products of aerobic respiration?
quiz.explain: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Glucose and oxygen are the reactants.

quiz.q: Where in a cell does most aerobic respiration happen?
quiz.explain: Mitochondria are where most aerobic respiration takes place.

quiz.q: Do plants respire?
quiz.explain: All living cells respire, day and night. In daylight, plants photosynthesise as well.

faq: What is the difference between respiration and photosynthesis?

Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide, water and light to make glucose and oxygen. Respiration uses glucose and oxygen to release energy, making carbon dioxide and water. In a way, one is the reverse of the other.
Why do my muscles ache after hard exercise?

Part of the reason is that during very hard exercise, your muscles respire without enough oxygen and make lactic acid. Scientists think other things, like tiny strains in the muscle, cause the ache a day or two later.

name: digestion
short: Digestion is how your body breaks down food into small, soluble molecules that can pass into your blood. Your teeth and stomach break food up, and enzymes break the big molecules into small ones.

sections.p: **Mouth**: teeth chew and saliva starts to digest starch. **Oesophagus**: a tube to the stomach. **Stomach**: churns food with acid, which kills most bacteria. **Small intestine**: digestion finishes and the small molecules pass into the blood. **Large intestine**: water is absorbed. What's left leaves through the anus.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up digestion. **Amylase** breaks starch into sugars. **Protease** breaks proteins into amino acids. **Lipase** breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Bile, made by the liver, breaks fat into tiny droplets so lipase can work faster.
The small intestine is about 6 metres long in an adult and its inside is covered in tiny finger-like **villi**. They give it a huge surface area, so digested food passes into the blood quickly.

examples: Bread tasting slightly sweet if you chew it for a long time, as amylase turns starch into sugar.
The stomach's acid killing bacteria in food.
Water being absorbed in the large intestine.
mistake: Thinking most digestion happens in the stomach. The stomach starts digesting protein, but most digestion and nearly all absorption of food happen in the small intestine.

quiz.q: Where are most digested food molecules absorbed into the blood?
quiz.explain: The villi in the small intestine give a huge surface area for absorption.

quiz.q: Which enzyme breaks down starch?
quiz.explain: Amylase breaks starch into sugars. It's in saliva and in the small intestine.

quiz.q: What is absorbed in the large intestine?
quiz.explain: The large intestine absorbs water from what's left of the food.

faq: How long does digestion take?
It varies a lot from person to person and meal to meal. Food usually spends a few hours in the stomach and small intestine, and the whole journey often takes one to three days.
Why do we need fibre if we can't digest it?
Fibre gives the muscles of the intestines something to push against, so food keeps moving through and you don't get constipated.

name: a balanced diet
short: A balanced diet means eating a variety of foods that give your body all the nutrients it needs, in the right amounts. No single food has everything.

sections.p: **Carbohydrates** (bread, rice, pasta) give energy. **Proteins** (meat, fish, beans, eggs) help you grow and repair. **Fats** (butter, oil, nuts) store energy and keep you warm. **Vitamins** and **minerals** (fruit, vegetables, milk) keep you healthy. **Fibre** (wholegrains, vegetables) keeps food moving through your gut. **Water** is needed by every cell.

You need only small amounts, but they matter. Calcium (in milk and cheese) helps build strong bones and teeth. Iron (in red meat, beans and leafy greens) helps your blood carry oxygen. Vitamin C (in oranges and peppers) keeps your skin and gums healthy.
If a diet is missing a nutrient for a long time, people can become ill. Long ago, sailors who ate no fruit or vegetables on long voyages got **scurvy** from a lack of vitamin C.

examples: A sandwich with wholemeal bread, cheese and salad covers several groups at once.
Beans are a good source of protein and fibre.
A glass of milk gives calcium and protein.
mistake: Thinking all fat is bad for you. Your body needs some fat: it stores energy, keeps you warm and helps you take in some vitamins. Balance means the right amount of each nutrient, not none of one.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is mainly for growth and repair?
quiz.explain: Proteins are used to build and repair cells, for example muscle.

quiz.q: Which mineral helps build strong bones and teeth?
quiz.explain: Calcium, found in milk, cheese and some green vegetables, builds bones and teeth.

faq: What is the Eatwell Guide?

It is the UK government's picture of a balanced diet. It shows roughly how much of what you eat should come from each food group, with fruit and vegetables and starchy foods making up the biggest parts.
How is the energy in food measured?
In kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal). You can find both on food labels.

name: the circulatory system
title: What is the circulatory system?
short: The circulatory system is your heart, your blood and your blood vessels. The heart pumps blood all round the body, carrying oxygen and food to every cell and taking waste away.

sections.p: Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It has four chambers and valves that stop blood flowing backwards. It beats all the time, even when you are asleep.

**Arteries** carry blood away from the heart and have thick, stretchy walls. **Veins** carry blood back to the heart and have valves. **Capillaries** are tiny vessels with very thin walls, where oxygen and food pass into the cells and carbon dioxide passes out.
Blood goes from the heart to the lungs to pick up oxygen, back to the heart, then out to the rest of the body, and back again. So blood passes through the heart twice on each trip round the body.

examples: Feeling your pulse in your wrist: that's an artery stretching each time your heart beats.
Red blood cells carrying oxygen from the lungs to your muscles.
Your heart beating faster when you run, to bring more oxygen to your muscles.
mistake: Thinking the blood in veins is blue. Blood is always red: it is bright red when it has lots of oxygen and darker red when it has less. Veins only look blue because of the way light passes through your skin.

quiz.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
quiz.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins carry it back.

quiz.q: Where does blood pick up oxygen?
quiz.explain: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs, then the heart pumps it to the rest of the body.

quiz.q: What carries oxygen in the blood?
quiz.explain: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.

faq: Why does my heart beat faster when I exercise?
Your muscles are respiring faster and need more oxygen and glucose. Your heart beats faster to carry more blood to them, and you breathe faster to take in more oxygen.
What are white blood cells for?
White blood cells help fight germs that get into your body. Platelets help your blood clot when you cut yourself.

name: an ecosystem
short: An ecosystem is all the living things in an area together with their non-living surroundings, like soil, water, light and temperature, and how they all affect each other.

sections.p: A **habitat** is the place where an organism lives. A **population** is all the organisms of one kind in an area, like all the rabbits in a field. A **community** is all the populations living together. The community plus the non-living things make the ecosystem.
Plants need light, water and minerals from the soil. Animals need food, water and shelter. If the non-living parts change, for example in a drought, the living things are affected too.
Living things in an ecosystem depend on each other. Bees need flowers for food, and many flowers need bees to carry their pollen. If one population changes, others in the food web change too.

examples: A pond, with its water, plants, insects, frogs and fish.
A woodland, with trees, fungi, birds, deer and soil.
A rock pool on the beach.
mistake: Thinking an ecosystem is only the living things. The non-living parts, like water, light, soil and temperature, are part of the ecosystem too.

quiz.q: What is a population?
options: All the organisms of one kind in an area
All the living things in an area
The place where an animal lives
quiz.explain: A population is one kind of organism: for example, all the frogs in a pond.

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-living part of an ecosystem?
quiz.explain: Sunlight isn't alive, but it is part of the ecosystem: plants need it to make food.

faq: Is a garden an ecosystem?
Yes. A garden has plants, insects, birds, worms and microorganisms living together with soil, water and light. Even a small pond or a log can be studied as an ecosystem.
What happens if one animal disappears from an ecosystem?
Its predators may have less food and its prey may increase. Because everything is linked in the food web, one change can spread through the whole ecosystem.

name: an adaptation
short: An adaptation is a feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat. Adaptations develop over many generations, not during one animal's life.

sections.p: Camels have wide feet that don't sink into sand, long eyelashes that keep sand out, and humps that store fat, which they can use for energy when food is scarce.
Polar bears have thick fur and a thick layer of fat under the skin to keep warm. Their pale fur helps them blend in with the snow and ice when they hunt.

Cacti have spines instead of wide leaves, so they lose less water. They store water in a thick stem and have wide roots to soak up rain quickly. Plants on a dark forest floor often have big leaves to catch more light.

examples: A cheetah's long legs and flexible spine for fast running.
A duck's webbed feet for swimming.
An owl's large eyes for seeing at night.
mistake: Thinking a camel's hump stores water. It stores fat. Camels survive without drinking for a long time because their bodies are very good at saving water.

quiz.q: Why do cacti have spines instead of wide leaves?
quiz.explain: Spines have a tiny surface, so very little water evaporates from them. They also protect the cactus from being eaten.

quiz.q: What does a camel's hump store?
quiz.explain: The hump is mostly fat, which can be used for energy.

quiz.q: How do adaptations come about?
options: When an animal decides to change
quiz.explain: Living things with useful features survive and have more young, so the features become more common over many generations. This is called natural selection.

faq: Can an animal adapt during its life?

An animal can change a little during its life, like a dog growing a thicker coat in winter, but the inherited features we call adaptations change slowly over many generations through natural selection.
Who explained how adaptations happen?
Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace both explained natural selection in the 1850s. Darwin's famous book about it, On the Origin of Species, was published in 1859.

name: sound
short: Sound is a vibration that travels through a solid, a liquid or a gas, like air, until it reaches your ear. Sound can't travel through empty space.

sections.p: Every sound starts with something vibrating: a guitar string, a drum skin or your vocal cords. The vibration makes the particles next to it vibrate, and they pass it on, all the way to your ear.

**Pitch** is how high or low a sound is. Faster vibrations (a higher **frequency**) make a higher pitch. Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). **Loudness** depends on how big the vibrations are (the **amplitude**). Loudness is measured in decibels (dB).

Sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air. It goes faster in water (about 1500 m/s) and faster still in solids like steel. Light is much, much faster, which is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder.

examples: A ruler twanging on a desk.
Hearing an echo when sound reflects off a cliff or a big wall.
Putting your ear to a table and hearing a tap clearly through the wood.
mistake: Thinking sound travels fastest through air. Sound needs particles to pass the vibration on, and in liquids and solids the particles are closer together, so sound travels faster in water than in air, and faster still in most solids.

quiz.q: Why can't sound travel through space?
options: There are no particles to vibrate
quiz.explain: Space is almost a vacuum, so there are no particles to pass the vibration on.

quiz.q: What makes a sound higher in pitch?
quiz.explain: A higher frequency (more vibrations each second) gives a higher pitch. Bigger vibrations make it louder, not higher.

quiz.q: In which does sound travel fastest?
quiz.explain: Sound travels fastest in solids like steel, then liquids, then gases. It can't travel through space at all.

faq: How can I tell how far away a storm is?
Count the seconds between the lightning and the thunder. Sound travels about 1 km in 3 seconds, so divide by 3 to get roughly how many kilometres away the storm is.
What can humans hear?
Young people can usually hear sounds from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. As people get older, they often can't hear the highest sounds any more. Dogs and bats can hear much higher sounds than we can.

name: magnetism
short: Magnetism is a non-contact force. Magnets attract things made of iron, nickel and cobalt, and two magnets can attract or repel each other without touching.

sections.p: Every magnet has a **north pole** and a **south pole**. Like poles repel (north pushes north away). Unlike poles attract (north pulls south). The force is strongest at the poles.
Only a few metals are magnetic: **iron**, **nickel** and **cobalt**, and steel, which is mostly iron. Most metals, like copper, aluminium, gold and silver, are not magnetic.
The space around a magnet where it pushes or pulls is its **magnetic field**. You can show it with iron filings or a small compass. The field lines go from the north pole to the south pole.

examples: A fridge magnet sticking to a steel door.
A compass needle pointing north.
Scrapyard cranes using electromagnets to lift cars.
mistake: Thinking all metals are magnetic. A magnet won't pick up a copper coin, an aluminium can or a gold ring. Only iron, nickel, cobalt and things made with them, like steel, are attracted.

quiz.q: What happens when you hold two north poles together?
quiz.explain: Like poles repel, so two north poles push each other away.

quiz.q: Which of these is attracted to a magnet?
quiz.explain: Steel is mostly iron, which is magnetic. Aluminium, copper and plastic are not.

faq: What is an electromagnet?
A coil of wire that becomes a magnet when electricity flows through it. It gets stronger with more turns of wire, more current, or an iron core inside, and you can switch it off.
Why does a compass point north?
The Earth acts like a giant magnet. The north pole of a compass needle is pulled towards the Arctic, so the needle lines up north to south.

name: electric current
title: What is electric current?
short: Electric current is a flow of electric charge around a circuit. In metal wires, the charge is carried by tiny particles called electrons. Current is measured in amps (A).

sections.p: Current can only flow if there is a complete loop with no gaps, from one end of the cell or battery, through the wires and components, and back to the other end. A switch works by making or breaking the gap.
A cell or battery gives the push, called the **voltage** (measured in volts, V). Components like bulbs and long thin wires make it harder for current to flow: they have **resistance**.
An **ammeter** measures current. It goes in the circuit in series, in the loop itself. In a simple series circuit the current is the same at every point.

examples: A torch: battery, switch and bulb in one loop.
A doorbell that only rings when the button completes the circuit.
A phone charger pushing current into a battery.
mistake: Thinking a bulb uses up the current, so less comes out than goes in. The current is the same all the way round a series circuit. What the bulb uses is energy: the current carries energy from the battery to the bulb.

quiz.q: What unit is current measured in?
quiz.explain: Current is measured in amps with an ammeter. Volts measure voltage.

quiz.q: Why does a bulb go out when you open a switch?
options: The circuit is no longer complete
quiz.explain: Opening the switch makes a gap, so current can't flow round the loop.

quiz.q: In a series circuit, how does the current after a bulb compare with the current before it?
quiz.explain: Current isn't used up. It is the same everywhere in a series circuit.

faq: Is it safe to experiment with electricity at home?
Only with small batteries, like AA cells, and with an adult. Never play with mains electricity from wall sockets: it can kill.
What is the difference between a cell and a battery?
A cell is one unit, like an AA. Strictly, a battery is two or more cells joined together, though people often call a single cell a battery.

name: speed
short: Speed is how far something travels in a certain time. You work it out with speed = distance ÷ time, and measure it in units like metres per second (m/s) or kilometres per hour (km/h).

sections.p: **speed = distance ÷ time**. If you run 100 m in 20 seconds, your speed is 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s. You can rearrange it: distance = speed × time, and time = distance ÷ speed.
Speed usually changes during a journey: a car speeds up, slows down and stops at lights. Distance ÷ time gives the **average speed** for the whole trip.
On a distance-time graph, a straight sloping line means a steady speed. The steeper the line, the faster the speed. A flat line means the object has stopped.

examples: A car travels 120 km in 2 hours: 120 ÷ 2 = 60 km/h.
A snail moves about 1 mm each second, which is 0.001 m/s.
Light travels about 300,000 km every second.
mistake: Mixing up units. If a distance is in metres and the time is in minutes, the answer is in metres per minute, not metres per second. Change the time to seconds first if you want m/s.

quiz.q: A cyclist rides 30 km in 2 hours. What is the average speed?
quiz.explain: speed = distance ÷ time = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 km/h.

quiz.q: On a distance-time graph, what does a flat line mean?
quiz.explain: A flat line means the distance isn't changing, so the object has stopped.

quiz.q: A runner keeps going at 4 m/s for 50 seconds. How far does she go?
quiz.explain: distance = speed × time = 4 × 50 = 200 m.

faq: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
Speed is just how fast. Velocity is speed in a certain direction. Two cars going at 50 km/h in opposite directions have the same speed but different velocities.
What is the fastest speed possible?
Nothing can travel faster than light in a vacuum, which is about 300,000 kilometres per second.

name: pressure
short: Pressure is how much a force is spread out over an area. The same force pressing on a small area makes a big pressure, and on a big area it makes a small pressure.

sections.p: **pressure = force ÷ area**. With the force in newtons (N) and the area in square metres (m²), the pressure is in newtons per square metre (N/m²), also called pascals (Pa).

A drawing pin has a tiny point, so a small push makes a huge pressure and it goes into a board easily. Snowshoes and wide tractor tyres spread the weight over a large area, so the pressure is low and they don't sink.

Water pressure gets bigger the deeper you go, which is why dams are thicker at the bottom. Air pressure comes from air particles hitting surfaces. The air around us presses on everything, but we don't notice because the pressure inside our bodies pushes back.

examples: A sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one because its edge has a smaller area.
A camel's wide feet stop it sinking into sand.
Your ears 'pop' on a plane as the air pressure changes.
mistake: Mixing up pressure and force. A person standing on one foot pushes down with the same force (their weight) as on two feet, but the pressure on the floor doubles because the area is halved.

quiz.q: A force of 100 N acts on an area of 2 m². What is the pressure?
quiz.explain: pressure = force ÷ area = 100 ÷ 2 = 50 N/m², which is 50 Pa.

quiz.q: Why are snowshoes wide?
options: To spread the weight and lower the pressure
To grip the snow with more force
quiz.explain: A bigger area means less pressure for the same weight, so you don't sink.

faq: Why is a dam thicker at the bottom?
Water pressure increases with depth, so the water pushes hardest on the bottom of the dam. The wall needs to be strongest there.
What is atmospheric pressure?
The pressure of the air around us. At sea level it is about 100,000 Pa. It gets lower as you go higher, which is why air is thinner on top of mountains.

name: renewable energy
short: Renewable energy comes from resources that won't run out, because nature keeps replacing them, like sunlight, wind and moving water. Fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas are non-renewable: once we use them up, they are gone.

sections.p: **Solar** (sunlight), **wind**, **hydroelectric** (water flowing from a dam), **tidal** and **wave** power, **geothermal** (heat from under the ground) and **biomass** (wood or crops, if new plants are grown to replace them).

**Coal**, **oil** and **natural gas** are fossil fuels: they formed from plants and animals over millions of years. **Nuclear** fuel (uranium) is also non-renewable. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which adds to climate change.

Renewables don't run out, and most don't release carbon dioxide while making electricity. But some depend on the weather: solar panels make less on cloudy days and wind turbines stop when there's no wind. So we also need ways to store energy.

examples: Wind turbines turning in the sea or on hills.
Solar panels on house roofs.
A hydroelectric dam in the mountains.
mistake: Thinking renewable means it has no effect on nature at all. Renewables are much cleaner to run, but building them has effects too: a hydroelectric dam floods a valley, and making solar panels and turbines uses materials and energy.

quiz.q: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
quiz.explain: Wind keeps blowing, so it won't run out. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels and are non-renewable.

quiz.q: Why is solar power not always available?
options: It needs sunlight, so it makes little at night
The Sun will run out next year
quiz.explain: Solar panels need light, so they make no electricity at night and less on cloudy days.

faq: Why are fossil fuels called fossil fuels?
They formed from the remains of plants and tiny sea creatures that lived millions of years ago, buried and squeezed underground, a bit like fossils.
Is nuclear power renewable?
No. Nuclear power stations use uranium, which is mined and will eventually run out. But they release very little carbon dioxide while running.

name: the seasons
title: What causes the seasons?
short: We have seasons because the Earth's axis is tilted. As the Earth travels round the Sun each year, first one half and then the other is tilted towards the Sun, and that half has summer.

sections.p: The Earth spins on an axis that is tilted by about 23.5 degrees. The tilt always points the same way in space as the Earth orbits the Sun, which takes one year.
When your half of the Earth is tilted towards the Sun, the Sun climbs higher in the sky, days are longer and sunlight hits the ground more directly, so it heats it more. That's summer.
When your half is tilted away, the Sun stays low, days are short and the sunlight is spread over a bigger area, so it heats less. That's winter. The other half of the Earth has the opposite season.

examples: In the UK it's summer in June, July and August, while in Australia it's winter.
Christmas comes in summer in New Zealand.
Near the equator there's little difference between summer and winter.
mistake: Thinking it's summer because the Earth is closer to the Sun. The Earth's distance from the Sun changes only a little, and the Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, which is winter in the UK.

quiz.q: What causes the seasons?
options: The tilt of the Earth's axis
The Earth getting closer to the Sun
quiz.explain: The tilt means each half of the Earth leans towards the Sun for part of the year.

quiz.q: When it is summer in the UK, what season is it in Australia?
quiz.explain: The UK is in the northern half of the Earth and Australia is in the southern half, so their seasons are opposite.

quiz.q: How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun?
quiz.explain: One orbit takes about 365¼ days, which is one year.

faq: Why are days longer in summer?
When your half of the Earth is tilted towards the Sun, it spends more of each spin of the Earth in sunlight, so days are longer and nights are shorter.
What causes day and night?
The Earth spinning on its axis once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day, and the side facing away has night.
